claim: Nematode-infected rootworm cadavers are attractive to rootworm larvae.
source: We found that nematode-infected rootworm cadavers are attractive to rootworm larvae, and that this behavior increases nematode reproductive success.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Attraction of rootworm larvae to nematode-infected cadavers increases nematode reproductive success.
source: We found that nematode-infected rootworm cadavers are attractive to rootworm larvae, and that this behavior increases nematode reproductive success.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Nematode-infected rootworms release distinct volatile bouquets, including butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT).
source: Nematode-infected rootworms release distinct volatile bouquets, including the unusual volatile butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: BHT alone attracts rootworms.
source: BHT alone attracts rootworms, and increases nematode reproductive success.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BHT increases nematode reproductive success.
source: BHT alone attracts rootworms, and increases nematode reproductive success.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Attraction of healthy hosts to nematode-infected cadavers is widespread across different species.
source: A screen of different nematode and herbivore species shows that attraction of healthy hosts to nematode-infected cadavers is widespread and likely involves species-specific volatile cues.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data across multiple species shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Attraction of healthy hosts to nematode-infected cadavers likely involves species-specific volatile cues.
source: A screen of different nematode and herbivore species shows that attraction of healthy hosts to nematode-infected cadavers is widespread and likely involves species-specific volatile cues.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by volatile analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Herbivore natural enemies protect plants by regulating herbivore populations.
source: Herbivore natural enemies protect plants by regulating herbivore populations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Herbivore natural enemies play a key role in terrestrial ecosystems by reducing herbivore abundance.
source: Herbivore natural enemies such as predators, parasites and parasitoids play a key role in terrestrial ecosystems by reducing herbivore abundance (Vidal and Murphy, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vidal and Murphy, 2018.

claim: Biological control relies on top-down control to protect crops from herbivores.
source: Biological control relies on this form of top-down control to protect crops from herbivores (Mills, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mills, 2001.

claim: Natural enemies have evolved various behavioral strategies to maximize their chances for host encounters.
source: Natural enemies have evolved various behavioral strategies to maximize their chances for host encounters (Jackson and Pollard, 1996; Olberg et al., 2000; de Rijk et al., 2013; de Rijk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Predators and parasitoids can use herbivore-induced plant volatiles to locate herbivores.
source: Predators and parasitoids for instance can use herbivore-induced plant volatiles to locate herbivores (Turlings et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turlings et al., 1990.

claim: Herbivores can detect and actively avoid contact with natural enemies.
source: Herbivores on the other hand can detect and actively avoid contact with natural enemies (Lima and Dill, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lima and Dill, 1990.

claim: Parasites with indirect life cycles can facilitate transfer to new hosts through host manipulation strategies.
source: Parasites with indirect life cycles can also facilitate the transfer to new hosts through host manipulation strategies, including changes in color, smell and behavior of their current hosts to attract alternate hosts (Mauck et al., 2010; Thomas et al., 2011; Daoust et al., 2015; Bakker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Insect bacterial pathogens can induce changes in volatile emissions in infected individuals, which results in the attraction of non-infected individuals.
source: Recent studies show that insect bacterial pathogens can induce to changes in volatile emissions in infected individuals, which results in the attraction of non-infected individuals (Keesey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keesey et al., 2017.

claim: Entomopathogenic nematodes are obligate pathogens of soil insects and important biological control agents of insect herbivores.
source: Entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) are obligate pathogens of soil insects and important biological control agents of insect herbivores (Grewal et al., 2005; Pilz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grewal et al., 2005 and Pilz et al., 2014.

claim: Infective juveniles (IJs) are the only EPN stage surviving in the soil looking for a host.
source: Infective juveniles (IJs) are the only EPN stage surviving in the soil looking for a host.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about EPN biology.

claim: IJs can locate a host using volatile cues that are emitted by herbivores and herbivore-infested plants.
source: IJs can locate a host using volatile cues that are emitted by herbivores and herbivore-infested plants (Rivera et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rivera et al., 2017.

claim: EPNs from the Steinernematidae and Heterorhabditidae families inoculate bacteria of the genus Xenorhabdus and Photorhabdus respectively, which kill the insect by septicemia and toxemia.
source: EPNs from the Steinernematidae and Heterorhabditidae families inoculate bacteria of the genus Xenorhabdus and Photorhabdus respectively, which kill the insect by septicemia and toxemia (Duchaud et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Duchaud et al., 2003.

claim: A crucial factor that determines the success of EPNs is their transmission efficiency from exploited to healthy hosts.
source: A crucial factor that determines the success of EPNs is their transmission efficiency from exploited to healthy hosts (Labaude and Griffin, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Labaude and Griffin, 2018.

claim: WCR can use plant toxins to repel H. bacteriophora.
source: WCR can use plant toxins to repel H. bacteriophora (Robert et al., 2017), but successful biological control of WCR through H. bacteriophora has been reported (Toepfer et al., 2005; Toepfer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robert et al., 2017.

claim: Successful biological control of WCR through H. bacteriophora has been reported.
source: WCR can use plant toxins to repel H. bacteriophora (Robert et al., 2017), but successful biological control of WCR through H. bacteriophora has been reported (Toepfer et al., 2005; Toepfer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Toepfer et al., 2005 and Toepfer et al., 2008.

claim: Maize+WCR+EPN complexes were attractive to WCR 48 hr after WCR and EPN application.
source: Maize+WCR+EPN complexes were attractive to WCR 48 hr after WCR and EPN application (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The attraction at 48 hr coincided with high root consumption by WCR.
source: The attraction coincided with high root consumption by WCR (Figure 1B) and high production of the WCR attractant (E)-β-caryophyllene (Robert et al., 2013; Robert et al., 2012a) by the attacked maize roots (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: (E)-β-caryophyllene is a WCR attractant.
source: The attraction coincided with high root consumption by WCR (Figure 1B) and high production of the WCR attractant (E)-β-caryophyllene (Robert et al., 2013; Robert et al., 2012a) by the attacked maize roots (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Robert et al., 2013 and Robert et al., 2012a.

claim: At 48 hr post infestation, approximately 30% of the WCR larvae were infected with EPNs.
source: At this time point, approx. 30% of the WCR larvae were infected with EPNs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: The attractive effect of maize-WCR-EPN complexes disappeared at 72 hr but reappeared at 96 hr.
source: The attractive effect of maize-WCR-EPN complexes disappeared at 72 hr but reappeared at 96 hr (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: At 96 hr post infestation, 95% of WCR larvae were infected and killed by EPNs.
source: The increased recruitment of WCR 96 hr post infestation was unexpected, as at this time point 95% of WCR larvae were infected and killed by EPNs (Figure 1D), and root removal and root (E)-β-caryophyllene emissions had decreased markedly (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Root removal and root (E)-β-caryophyllene emissions had decreased markedly at 96 hr post infestation.
source: The increased recruitment of WCR 96 hr post infestation was unexpected, as at this time point 95% of WCR larvae were infected and killed by EPNs (Figure 1D), and root removal and root (E)-β-caryophyllene emissions had decreased markedly (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Plants in the presence of WCR or EPNs alone were not attractive to WCR at 96 hr post infection.
source: Plants in the presence of WCR or EPNs alone were not attractive to WCR than plants alone at this time point.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Plants in the presence of WCR under EPN attack were attractive to WCR larvae at 96 hr post infection.
source: However, plants in the presence of WCR under EPN attack were attractive to WCR larvae (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: WCR larvae preferred EPN-infected WCR cadavers over uninfected cadavers.
source: WCR larvae preferred EPN-infected WCR cadavers over uninfected cadavers (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The attraction to EPN-infected cadavers was strongest 96 hr after infection, shortly before the emergence of IJs.
source: Time course analysis revealed that the attraction to EPN-infected cadavers was strongest 96 hr after infection, shortly before the emergence of IJs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: WCR larvae visited infected cadavers more often than uninfected cadavers.
source: WCR larvae visited infected cadavers more often than uninfected cadavers (Figure 1G) and spent more time per visit on infected cadavers (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: WCR larvae spent more time per visit on infected cadavers than uninfected cadavers.
source: WCR larvae visited infected cadavers more often than uninfected cadavers (Figure 1G) and spent more time per visit on infected cadavers (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: The number of root visits was increased for roots that were close to infected cadavers.
source: The number of root visits was also increased for roots that were close to infected cadavers (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: WCR larvae did not show any preference for uninfected or EPN-infected cadavers in the absence of plant roots.
source: WCR larvae did not show any preference for uninfected or EPN-infected cadavers in the absence of plant roots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: WCR larvae did not show any preference for roots previously exposed to uninfected or EPN-infected cadavers.
source: WCR larvae did not show any preference for the different roots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EPN infection of WCR directly increases volatile-mediated recruitment and cadaver contact of healthy foraging WCR larvae.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that EPN infection of WCR directly increases volatile-mediated recruitment and cadaver contact of healthy foraging WCR larvae.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in Figure 1 and its supplements.

claim: Two times more WCR larvae were recovered in the vicinity of EPN-infected cadavers compared to control cadavers in soil arenas.
source: Two times more WCR larvae were recovered in the vicinity of EPN-infected cadavers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: EPN infection rates were higher on the side where EPN-infected cadavers were buried.
source: Furthermore, EPN infection rates were higher on the side where EPN-infected cadavers were buried (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of emerging EPN juveniles per larva was similar on both sides of the arena.
source: The number of emerging EPN juveniles was similar on both sides (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Three times more EPN offspring emerged on the side with EPN-infected cadavers.
source: Overall, three times more EPN offspring emerged on the side with EPN-infected cadavers (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: There was no significant difference in CO2 emissions between uninfected and EPN-infected WCR cadavers.
source: GC-FID analysis revealed no significant difference in CO2 emissions between uninfected and EPN-infected WCR cadavers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Headspace SPME and GC-MS analysis revealed 279 distinct volatile features from WCR cadavers, including 15 features exclusively detected in the headspace of infected cadavers.
source: Headspace solid phase micro extraction (SPME) and GC-MS followed by automated alignment and peak picking revealed 279 distinct volatile features, including 15 features that were exclusively detected in the headspace of infected cadavers (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed a clear separation of volatile profiles from infected and uninfected cadavers along PC axis 1.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed a clear separation of volatile profiles from infected and uninfected cadavers along PC axis 1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: A single volatile eluding at 18.23 min explained 45.6% of the variability of PC axis one and was exclusively present in the headspace of infected cadavers.
source: A single volatile eluding at 18.23 min explained 45.6% of the variability of axis one and was exclusively present in the headspace of infected cadavers (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: 9 out of 11 integrated peaks were emitted in higher quantities by infected cadavers.
source: Additional manual integration and relative quantification of the 11 highest peaks in the headspace chromatograms revealed that 9 out of 11 integrated peaks were emitted in higher quantities by infected cadavers (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: The compound at retention time 18.23 min was identified as butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT).
source: Based on comparisons of retention times, mass spectra and co-injection of a synthetic standard, the compound was identified as butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and based on analytical chemistry methods.

claim: No BHT was detected in blank controls and in the headspace of different materials used for rearing and experimentation.
source: No BHT was detected in blank controls and in the headspace of different materials that were used for rearing and experimentation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and based on experimental controls.

claim: Environmental contamination as a source of BHT can be excluded.
source: Thus, environmental contamination as a source of BHT can be excluded.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of BHT in controls.

claim: A single infected WCR cadaver releases up to 5 ng of BHT per hr.
source: A single infected WCR cadaver was found to release up to 5 ng of BHT per hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BHT starts being released 72 hr after EPN infection.
source: Emission kinetics showed that BHT starts being released 72 hr after EPN infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which corresponds to the onset of increased WCR recruitment to EPN-infected cadavers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BHT has originally been described as a synthetic antioxidant.
source: BHT has originally been described as a synthetic antioxidant (Babu and Wu, 2008), but has also been identified in the headspace of cyanobacteria, algae, and fungal pathogens (Babu and Wu, 2008; Hussaini et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Babu and Wu, 2008.

claim: BHT has been identified in the headspace of cyanobacteria, algae, and fungal pathogens.
source: BHT has originally been described as a synthetic antioxidant (Babu and Wu, 2008), but has also been identified in the headspace of cyanobacteria, algae, and fungal pathogens (Babu and Wu, 2008; Hussaini et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Babu and Wu, 2008 and Hussaini et al., 2011.

claim: No BHT release from P. laumondii infected WCR cadavers was detected.
source: No BHT release from P. laumondii infected WCR cadavers was detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: P. laumondii grown in vitro did not release any BHT.
source: P. laumondii grown in vitro did not release any BHT either (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No BHT release from EPNs was detected.
source: We also did not detect any BHT release from EPNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) or uninfected WCR cadavers (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: BHT was exclusively detected in EPN-infected WCR cadavers.
source: Instead, BHT was exclusively detected in EPN-infected WCR cadavers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: BHT release is specific to infection of WCR by EPNs.
source: These results imply that BHT release is specific to infection of WCR by EPNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing BHT is only detected in EPN-infected WCR cadavers.

claim: At physiologically relevant doses, synthetic BHT was attractive to WCR and elicited responses comparable to infected cadavers.
source: At physiologically relevant doses, synthetic BHT was attractive to WCR and elicited responses that were comparable to infected cadavers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: BHT complementation of uninfected WCR cadavers rendered them as attractive as infected cadavers.
source: Furthermore, BHT complementation of uninfected WCR cadavers rendered them as attractive as infected cadavers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: BHT is sufficient to attract WCR to nematode infected cadavers.
source: Thus, BHT is sufficient to attract WCR to nematode infected cadavers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing BHT alone attracts WCR.

claim: Pre-exposure of WCR to BHT increased infection rates by 19%.
source: Pre-exposure of WCR to BHT increased infection rates by 19% (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The increased infection rate was not due to increased attraction of EPNs to BHT-exposed larvae.
source: The increased infection rate was not due to increased attraction of EPNs, as the amounts of BHT released by BHT-exposed larvae was not sufficient to trigger a preference choice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pre-exposure of EPNs to BHT did not affect their capacity to infect WCR.
source: By contrast, pre-exposure of EPNs to BHT did not affect their capacity to infect WCR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: EPNs were attracted by EPN-infected cadavers as well as BHT similar to WCR.
source: Interestingly, EPNs were attracted by EPN-infected cadavers as well as BHT similar to WCR (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: In addition to attracting WCR larvae, BHT increases EPN infection success and attracts EPNs themselves.
source: Thus, in addition to attracting WCR larvae, BHT increases EPN infection success and attracts EPNs themselves.

claim: Significantly more WCR larvae were recovered in the vicinity of BHT presence in soil arenas.
source: Significantly more WCR larvae were recovered in the vicinity of BHT presence (Figure 5B), confirming the attractive effect of BHT in soil.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The proportion of EPN-infected WCR larvae was twice higher on the BHT supplemented side.
source: The proportion of EPN-infected WCR larvae was twice higher on the BHT supplemented side (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: The number of EPN juveniles emerging per larva was similar between the larvae from both sides of the BHT experiment.
source: The number of EPN juveniles emerging per larva was similar between the larvae from both sides (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Three times more nematodes of the next generation emerged from the BHT side.
source: Overall, three times more nematodes of the next generation emerged from the BHT side (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: BHT enhances the recruitment of healthy WCR larvae, and increases the predation success and total offspring production of EPNs.
source: Thus, BHT enhances the recruitment of healthy WCR larvae, and increases the predation success and total offspring production of EPNs.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in Figure 5.

claim: Application of EPNs to one side of the arena led to G. melonella infection of the other side, and the infection rate was slightly increased when BHT was added.

evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed increase in nematode reproduction in response to cadavers as well as pure BHT is likely to be the result of increased WCR recruitment, increased infection rates and increased EPN recruitment.
source: Thus, the observed increase in nematode reproduction in response to cadavers as well as pure BHT is likely to be the result of increased WCR recruitment, increased infection rates and increased EPN recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Five of the seven tested species were attracted to cadavers of EPN-infected conspecifics.
source: Five of the seven tested species, including Diabrotica virgifera (WCR), D. balteata, Tenebrio molitor, Drosophila melanogaster and Spodoptera littoralis were attracted to cadavers of EPN-infected conspecifics (Figure 6A).

claim: Galleria melonella larvae preferred non-infected over infected cadavers.

claim: WCR larvae were attracted to WCR cadavers infested by H. bacteriophora, H. beicherriana, H. georgiana and S. feltiae.

claim: WCR larvae were attracted to all four tested species of EPN-infected cadavers (D. balteata, T. molitor, S. littoralis, G. mellonella).

claim: Only the closely related D. balteata was attracted to infected WCR cadavers.

claim: Attraction of herbivores to infected cadavers is widespread, with the specificity of attraction varying between insect species.
source: Thus, attraction of herbivores to infected cadavers is widespread, with the specificity of attraction varying between insect species.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in Figure 6.

claim: EPN infection significantly altered the volatile bouquets of all tested insects.
source: EPN infection significantly altered the volatile bouquets of all insects (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: EPN-induced volatiles differed substantially between species.
source: EPN-induced volatiles differed substantially between species.

claim: BHT was only released from EPN-infected WCR and D. melanogaster cadavers.
source: BHT was only released from EPN-infected WCR and D. melanogaster cadavers.

claim: Parasites have developed diverse strategies to manipulate their hosts and thereby increase their fitness.
source: Parasites have developed diverse strategies to manipulate their hosts and thereby increase their fitness (Moore, 2002; Thomas et al., 2005; Poulin and Maure, 2015).

claim: Volatiles from infected cadavers attract healthy herbivores and increases nematode infection success.

claim: These phenomena markedly increase top-down control of herbivores in the soil, as shown for the western corn rootworm.
source: Together, these phenomena markedly increase top-down control of herbivores in the soil, as shown here for an important agricultural pest, the western corn rootworm.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Babu and Wu, 2008 and Vikram et al., 2004.
